questions.explain: RDS for SQL Server has no read replicas, so read scale-out for SQL Server is via AG secondaries, platform replicas, and DR standbys — each with its own cost model.
options: AG secondaries are unavailable for RDS for SQL Server entirely
Read replicas are cheaper than AG secondaries because storage is shared
RDS for SQL Server has no read replicas — the scale-out copies are AG secondaries, platform replicas, and DR standbys
RDS read replicas can be promoted for reporting but not for DR
questions.q: How does SQL Server's secondary story differ from 'read replica economics' on other engines?

questions.explain: A secondary's total cost has four components: compute (often the largest line), storage (full copy plus IOPS tier), licensing (SA secondary rights must be verified), and transfer (cross-region replication is metered).
options: Compute, storage, and support plan level
Compute, storage, licensing, and transfer
vCores, memory, throughput, and snapshot retention
Instance hours, I/O requests, data transfer, and backup storage
questions.q: What are the four cost components of a secondary copy?

questions.explain: A readable secondary pays for itself when it absorbs a workload that would otherwise force a primary upsizing — a half-size secondary is cheaper than doubling the primary.
options: When reporting consists of a handful of queries per day
When the secondary absorbs a workload that would otherwise force a primary upsizing
When the secondary is sized identically to the primary 'for safety' while serving 5% of its load
When the primary is idle and there's nothing to offload
questions.q: When does a readable secondary actually pay for itself?

questions.explain: Correct routing requires ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly (or read-scale endpoints) plus lag-aware routing; the unrouted secondary — paid for, receiving no traffic — is the most common waste.
options: A secondary sized smaller than the primary
A secondary running in a different AZ than the primary
A readable DR secondary that also serves reporting traffic
An unrouted secondary — provisioned and paid for, but receiving no traffic
questions.q: What does the chapter call the most common waste among secondaries?

questions.explain: A DR standby that never serves traffic is pure insurance — but a readable DR secondary that also serves reads converts insurance into infrastructure, the best economics in the chapter when RPO/RTO allow async.
options: Backup-based DR, because it is always cheaper than any standby
A DR secondary that also serves reads — dual-use converts insurance into infrastructure
A stopped VM with attached storage, because it can scale instantly
The standby should never serve reads to preserve its recovery role
questions.q: What is the best DR standby economics pattern when RPO/RTO allow async replication?
